subject: obstetrics-gynaecology
title: Postpartum haemorrhage: atony, trauma, tissue and thrombin

steps.tx: **Postpartum haemorrhage** remains one of the fastest killers in obstetrics, defined as blood loss of 500 ml after vaginal birth and 1000 ml after caesarean section. The causes group into the **four Ts**, namely atonic uterus, genital tract trauma, retained tissue and clotting failure. **Active management of the third stage** with oxytocin 10 IU given intramuscularly, controlled cord traction and uterine massage prevents many cases. Risk rises with grand multiparity, twins, polyhydramnios and macrosomia, so quantified drapes and shock index guide transfusion.
steps.say: Postpartum haemorrhage means bleeding of 500 ml after a vaginal birth and 1000 ml after a caesarean section. Four groups of causes explain most cases, and the atonic uterus leads the list. Active management of the third stage prevents many cases because oxytocin contracts the uterus firmly. Measured drapes estimate the loss while rising pulse and falling pressure warn that transfusion is needed.

steps.tx: **Oxytocin** stays first line for atony, given as 10 IU intramuscularly for prevention and as a 20 to 40 IU infusion for treatment, while rapid bolus injection can cause hypotension. When bleeding continues, **ergometrine** follows except in hypertension because it raises pressure and causes nausea. **Carboprost** comes next except in asthma because it provokes bronchospasm with diarrhoea and fever, and misoprostol 800 given sublingually causes shivering and fever. Tranexamic acid 1 g given intravenously within 3 hours reduces clot breakdown, while bimanual and aortic compression bridge the gap.
steps.say: Oxytocin remains the first drug because it contracts the uterus quickly and reliably. Ergometrine follows when bleeding continues, but doctors withhold it when the mother has hypertension. Carboprost comes next, but doctors avoid it when the mother has asthma. Tranexamic acid 1 g given intravenously within 3 hours slows clot breakdown, while firm bimanual compression controls bleeding until drugs act.

steps.tx: The illustration shows a contracting postpartum uterus receiving an **oxytocin infusion**, alongside vials of oxytocin, ergometrine and carboprost with warning icons for their contraindications. Oxytocin 10 IU given intramuscularly starts prevention and a 20 to 40 IU infusion treats established atony. **Ergometrine** stays contraindicated in hypertension and **carboprost** stays contraindicated in asthma, and the red crossed icons fix this pairing for recall. For the exam, match each drug to its ban before choosing the next uterotonic.
steps.say: The illustration shows a contracting uterus with an oxytocin infusion running into a vein. Three vials stand beside it, and crossed icons warn that ergometrine harms hypertension while carboprost harms asthma. Examiners love this pairing because choosing the wrong second drug injures the mother. Always confirm blood pressure and chest history before stepping beyond oxytocin.

steps.tx: When drugs fail, **balloon tamponade** with a Bakri balloon or a low resource condom catheter controls bleeding for up to 24 hours with antibiotic cover. **Compression sutures** such as the B Lynch stitch, followed by uterine artery and then internal iliac ligation, preserve the uterus stepwise. **Hysterectomy** remains the last resort when bleeding stays uncontrollable. Retained tissue needs manual exploration, especially with a succenturiate lobe, while placenta accreta spectrum after previous sections with bladder invasion needs planned hysterectomy.
steps.say: Balloon tamponade presses the cavity from within and buys up to 24 hours when drugs fail. Compression stitches and artery ties follow in sequence because each step preserves the uterus. Hysterectomy remains the final option when bleeding refuses to stop. Retained tissue needs manual removal, while suspected accreta needs a planned hysterectomy.

steps.tx: **Disseminated intravascular coagulation** complicates abruption, amniotic fluid embolism, sepsis and massive transfusion through dilution, and it needs fibrinogen replacement with cryoprecipitate guided by clotting tests. **Massive transfusion** uses O negative blood in emergency, warms fluids with calcium replacement, and follows a 1 to 1 to 1 ratio of red cells, plasma and platelets, with early tranexamic acid and cell salvage where available. **Uterine inversion** presents with shock out of proportion and needs urgent replacement by the Johnson manoeuvre, with relaxants before oxytocics. Every PPH deserves audit.
steps.say: Clotting failure follows abruption, embolism, sepsis and dilution from heavy transfusion. Resuscitation uses warmed blood with calcium and a balanced ratio of red cells, plasma and platelets. Uterine inversion declares itself through shock that exceeds visible loss, and it needs urgent manual replacement. Teams should audit every major bleed so system gaps get fixed.
